name: Sapporo
summary: Hokkaido's capital is a grid of wide streets built for snow. Eat your way through ramen, crab and soup curry, and add a day trip to the canal town of Otaru.
seasonNote: The Snow Festival in early February is the peak; summer is cool and dry while the rest of Japan swelters.
arrival: Rapid trains run from New Chitose Airport to Sapporo Station in about 40 minutes.
gettingAround: Three subway lines and a streetcar loop cover the centre; underground walkways link Sapporo Station to Susukino in winter.
cashTip: IC cards and credit cards work widely; small ramen counters use cash ticket machines.
foodTip: Try miso ramen, soup curry, jingisukan grilled lamb, fresh crab and soft-serve ice cream.
buyTip: Shiroi Koibito biscuits, Royce chocolate and Hokkaido dairy sweets.

connections.note: One of the world's busiest air routes; add transfers at both ends.

items.name: Odori Park and Sapporo TV Tower
items.summary: A 1.5 km strip of park through the city centre, home to the Snow Festival, with a tower viewpoint at one end.
items.expect: Snow sculptures in February and beer gardens in summer.
items.tip: Go up the TV Tower at dusk to see the park lit along its length.
items.why: It is the stage for every major Sapporo event.
flow: Walk the park from west to east.
Go up the TV Tower.

items.name: Sapporo Beer Museum
items.summary: A red-brick 1890 brewery building telling the story of Japan's oldest beer brand, with a tasting hall.
items.expect: Free to enter; tastings are paid.
items.tip: Follow with jingisukan lamb in the beer hall next door.
items.why: Beer is part of the city's identity, and the building is handsome.
flow: Walk the free exhibition.
Order the three-beer tasting set.

items.name: Mount Moiwa
items.summary: A 531-metre summit reached by ropeway and mini cable car, with a night view of the whole city.
items.expect: Cold and windy at the top; queues at sunset.
items.tip: Go up just before dusk and stay for the lights.
items.why: It is rated one of Japan's best night views.
flow: Streetcar to the ropeway shuttle.
Ride up for sunset.

items.name: Hokkaido Shrine and Maruyama Park
items.summary: The island's main Shinto shrine, in a forest park famous for cherry blossom in early May.
items.expect: Quiet most days; busy at New Year and blossom time.
items.tip: Combine it with coffee in the Maruyama neighbourhood.
items.why: A calm, wooded contrast to the city grid.
flow: Walk through the park from Maruyama-koen station.
Visit the shrine.

items.name: Shiroi Koibito Park
items.summary: A whimsical biscuit factory with a production line view, sweets workshops and gardens.
items.expect: Family-oriented and sweet-themed.
items.tip: Book a biscuit-decorating session if travelling with children.
items.why: It is the home of Hokkaido's best-known souvenir.
flow: Walk the factory tour.
Have a parfait in the café.

items.name: Otaru
items.summary: A port town with a lamp-lit canal, stone warehouses, glass shops and sushi.
items.expect: Tour groups on the canal at midday.
items.tip: Sit on the right side of the train for sea views and stay until the gas lamps come on.
items.why: It is the easiest and prettiest day trip from Sapporo.
flow: Train from Sapporo, about 35 minutes.
Walk the canal and Sakaimachi Street, then eat sushi.

items.name: Ganso Ramen Yokocho
items.summary: A narrow alley of about 17 tiny ramen counters, the birthplace of Sapporo miso ramen.
items.expect: Counter seats only and short queues at night.
items.tip: Order miso ramen with butter and corn.
items.why: Miso ramen was invented in Sapporo, and this alley made it famous.
flow: Walk the alley and pick a counter.
Order miso ramen.
order: Miso ramen with butter and corn

items.name: Soup Curry Garaku
items.summary: A popular soup curry restaurant serving rich broth with vegetables and chicken.
items.expect: Queues of 30 to 60 minutes at lunch.
items.tip: Take a number early; choose your spice level and rice size.
items.why: Soup curry is Sapporo's own dish and this is a well-loved version.
flow: Take a queue ticket.
Order chicken and vegetable soup curry.
order: Chicken leg and vegetable soup curry

items.name: Sapporo Beer Garden
items.summary: Beer halls in the old brewery serving all-you-can-eat grilled lamb.
items.expect: Smoky; your clothes will smell of the grill.
items.tip: Book the Kessel Hall and use the bags provided for coats.
items.why: Jingisukan with fresh draught beer is the classic Hokkaido meal.
flow: Reserve a slot.
Grill lamb and vegetables on the dome pan.

items.name: Nijo Market
items.summary: A compact seafood market with stalls and small diners serving crab, sea urchin and rice bowls.
items.expect: Tourist prices; best in the morning.
items.tip: Have a kaisendon seafood rice bowl for breakfast.
items.why: Hokkaido seafood is the best in Japan.
flow: Browse the crab and scallop stalls.
Sit down for a seafood bowl.

name: Kanazawa
tagline: Gardens, geisha streets and gold leaf
summary: A castle town that escaped wartime bombing, so its samurai and geisha districts survive. Two days cover the garden, the old quarters and the market at an easy pace.
seasonNote: Winters are wet and snowy but beautiful, with the garden's trees roped against the snow.
arrival: The Hokuriku Shinkansen runs direct from Tokyo in about 2.5 to 3 hours.
gettingAround: Loop buses circle the sights from the station; the centre is also walkable.
cashTip: Carry some cash for market stalls and small teahouses.
foodTip: Try a kaisendon at the market, nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), jibuni duck stew and gold-leaf ice cream.
buyTip: Gold leaf goods, Kutani porcelain and Kaga-yuzen dyed silk.

connections.note: Shinkansen to Tsuruga, then a limited express; one change.
Shinkansen to Tsuruga, then a limited express; one change.

items.name: Kenroku-en
items.summary: One of Japan's three great landscape gardens, with ponds, teahouses and a famous two-legged stone lantern.
items.expect: Tour groups mid-morning.
items.tip: Arrive at opening; early-morning entry before ticket hours is free.
items.why: It was designed to be beautiful in every season.
flow: Enter from the castle side.
Circle Kasumigaike pond and stop at a teahouse.

items.name: Kanazawa Castle Park
items.summary: The white-walled gates and turrets of the Maeda lords' castle, carefully rebuilt in timber.
items.expect: Large open grounds; the reconstructed buildings are ticketed.
items.tip: Enter by the Ishikawa Gate straight from Kenroku-en.
items.why: The joinery inside the turrets shows traditional carpentry at full scale.
flow: Cross from the garden through Ishikawa Gate.
See the Gojikken Nagaya storehouse.

items.name: Higashi Chaya District
items.summary: A preserved geisha quarter of latticed wooden teahouses, some open to visit.
items.expect: Crowded in the afternoon; many shops sell gold-leaf sweets.
items.tip: Visit Shima teahouse, then stay until dusk when the street empties.
items.why: It is the best-preserved teahouse district outside Kyoto.
flow: Walk the main street.
Tour Shima teahouse and try matcha.

items.name: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art
items.wiki: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa
items.summary: A circular glass museum known for Leandro Erlich's Swimming Pool installation.
items.expect: The pool's lower level needs a same-day reservation.
items.tip: Reserve the pool slot online in the morning.
items.why: It is one of Japan's most popular contemporary museums.
flow: See the free public zones.
Enter the Swimming Pool at your slot.

items.name: Nagamachi Samurai District
items.summary: Lanes of earthen walls and canals where samurai families lived, with the Nomura house open to visit.
items.expect: A short walk; walls are covered with straw mats in winter.
items.tip: Go inside the Nomura residence for its small garden.
items.why: It shows how the samurai class lived in a castle town.
flow: Walk the canal-side lanes.
Visit the Nomura house.

items.name: D.T. Suzuki Museum
items.summary: A minimalist museum to the Zen philosopher, built around a still reflecting pool.
items.expect: Small and quiet; more a space than a collection.
items.tip: Sit by the Water Mirror Garden for a few minutes.
items.why: A calm, beautiful piece of modern architecture.
flow: Pass through the exhibition space.
Sit in the contemplative space by the water.

items.name: Omicho Market
items.summary: Kanazawa's 300-year-old covered market, with seafood stalls and rice-bowl restaurants.
items.expect: Queues at the famous bowl shops by 11 am.
items.tip: Come early; many restaurants close mid-afternoon and on Wednesdays.
items.why: Sea of Japan seafood here rivals anywhere in the country.
flow: Walk the aisles and try an oyster or croquette.
Queue for a kaisendon.

items.name: Mori Mori Sushi Omicho
items.summary: A popular conveyor-belt sushi restaurant using local Sea of Japan fish.
items.expect: A numbered queue at peak times.
items.tip: Order the three-piece local fish sets from the touch panel.
items.why: High-quality sushi at conveyor prices.
flow: Take a number.
Order nodoguro and the local set.
items.best: Outside the busiest lunch or dinner hour.

items.name: Hakuichi gold leaf ice cream
items.summary: Soft-serve ice cream wrapped in a whole sheet of edible gold leaf.
items.expect: A photo stop more than a flavour experience.
items.tip: Eat it inside; the leaf blows away in wind.
items.why: Kanazawa makes nearly all of Japan's gold leaf.
flow: Order at the counter.
Eat in the shop's seating area.

name: Fukuoka
tagline: Ramen stalls and an easy-going port city
summary: Kyushu's biggest city is about eating: tonkotsu ramen, open-air yatai stalls and seafood. Sights are few and close together, and Dazaifu's shrine is a half-day trip.
seasonNote: Summer is hot and humid; the Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival runs in early July.
arrival: The airport is five minutes by subway from Hakata Station.
gettingAround: The subway links the airport, Hakata and Tenjin; most of the centre is walkable.
cashTip: Bring cash for yatai stalls, which rarely take cards.
foodTip: Try Hakata tonkotsu ramen, mentaiko (spicy cod roe), motsunabe offal hotpot and mizutaki chicken hotpot.
buyTip: Mentaiko to take home (chilled), Hakata dolls and Hakata-ori woven textiles.
via: Direct flights from much of Asia, otherwise via Tokyo or Osaka

connections.note: High-speed ferry; flights take under an hour.

items.name: Dazaifu Tenmangu
items.summary: A major shrine to the god of learning, approached over arched bridges through plum trees.
items.expect: Students praying for exams and a shop-lined approach.
items.tip: Try a grilled umegae mochi on the approach and see the Kengo Kuma-designed café.
items.why: It is Kyushu's most important shrine.
flow: Train from Tenjin, about 30 minutes.
Cross the bridges to the main hall.

items.name: Ohori Park
items.summary: A large pond crossed by island bridges, with a Japanese garden and castle ruins next door.
items.expect: Joggers and families; calm on weekdays.
items.tip: Walk the causeway across the pond, then climb to the Fukuoka Castle ruins.
items.why: The city's favourite green space, lovely at cherry blossom time.
flow: Cross the pond by the islands.
Continue to the castle ruins viewpoint.

items.name: Kushida Shrine
items.summary: Hakata's guardian shrine, displaying a towering Yamakasa festival float all year.
items.expect: A short stop in the old town.
items.tip: Pair it with the Hakata Machiya Folk Museum across the lane.
items.why: It is the heart of the city's biggest festival.
flow: See the main hall.
Find the decorated float at the back.

items.name: Canal City Hakata
items.summary: A curving shopping complex built around an indoor canal with fountain shows.
items.expect: A mall, with a ramen floor on level five.
items.tip: Use the Ramen Stadium to compare styles from around Japan.
items.why: A handy rainy-day stop between Hakata and Nakasu.
flow: Watch a fountain show.
Go up to the Ramen Stadium.

items.name: Fukuoka Tower and Momochi Seaside Park
items.summary: A mirrored 234-metre tower beside an artificial beach, with a view over the bay.
items.expect: A bus ride from the centre.
items.tip: Time your visit for sunset over the bay.
items.why: It is the best high view of the city and coast.
flow: Bus to the tower.
Go up, then walk the beach.

items.name: Nanzoin Temple
items.summary: A hillside temple with a 41-metre bronze reclining Buddha.
items.expect: Modest dress is required; large groups may be refused.
items.tip: Take the train to Kido Nanzoin-mae, 25 minutes from Hakata.
items.why: The statue is one of the largest bronzes in the world.
flow: Walk up from the station through the temple grounds.
Reach the reclining Buddha.

items.name: Nakasu yatai stalls
items.summary: A riverside row of open-air food stalls serving ramen, skewers and oden from dusk.
items.expect: Eight to ten seats per stall; closed in heavy rain.
items.tip: Check posted prices, order a drink and a few dishes, then move on.
items.why: Fukuoka has more yatai than the rest of Japan combined.
flow: Walk the row from about 7 pm.
Squeeze in and order ramen and yakitori.

items.name: Ichiran Main Building
items.summary: The flagship of the tonkotsu ramen chain known for solo booths and a custom order sheet.
items.expect: Queues at peak hours; open around the clock.
items.tip: Fill in the form: firm noodles, and extra noodles (kaedama) afterwards.
items.why: It is an easy, English-friendly start to Hakata ramen in its home city.
flow: Buy a ticket at the machine.
Fill in the preference sheet in your booth.

items.name: Hakata Motsunabe Yamanaka
items.summary: A well-known restaurant for motsunabe, a hotpot of beef offal, cabbage and garlic chives.
items.expect: Reservations advised; offal is the point.
items.tip: Choose the miso broth and finish with champon noodles.
items.why: Motsunabe is Fukuoka's winter comfort food.
flow: Reserve a table.
Order the miso hotpot and finish with noodles.

name: Phuket
tagline: Beaches, islands and a Sino-Portuguese old town
summary: Pick a beach to match your pace, spend one day on a boat to Phang Nga Bay or the Phi Phi islands, and save an evening for Phuket Old Town's food.
seasonNote: May to October is monsoon season, with rough west-coast seas and red-flag days.
arrival: The airport is in the north; allow 45 to 90 minutes by taxi or shared minibus to the beaches.
gettingAround: Distances are long and taxis costly; use ride-hailing apps or the Smart Bus along the west coast.
cashTip: Carry baht for beach vendors, markets and tuk-tuks; ATMs charge a fixed foreign-card fee.
foodTip: Try Hokkien noodles, moo hong braised pork, dim sum breakfast and southern crab curry with rice noodles.
buyTip: Cashew nuts, batik and local pearls from established shops.
baseArea: Kata or Karon for families; Kamala or Bang Tao for quiet; Old Town for food

items.name: Phang Nga Bay
items.summary: A bay of limestone towers rising from green water, explored by boat and sea kayak.
items.expect: James Bond Island is crowded; boats vary a lot in quality.
items.tip: Choose a small-group or late-start tour that includes kayaking the sea caves.
items.why: It is one of Thailand's most striking seascapes.
flow: Boat from the east-coast piers.
Kayak the lagoons and stop at a floating village.

items.name: Phi Phi Islands
items.summary: Cliff-ringed islands with clear water for snorkelling, including Maya Bay.
items.expect: A long speedboat day; Maya Bay has visitor limits and closes for part of the low season.
items.tip: Take an early-bird tour to reach Maya Bay before the crowds.
items.why: The islands have the clearest water and most dramatic cliffs in the region.
flow: Speedboat from Phuket.
Maya Bay, snorkelling stops and lunch on Phi Phi Don.

items.name: Phuket Old Town
items.summary: Streets of pastel Sino-Portuguese shophouses, shrines, cafés and street art.
items.expect: Hot at midday; Sunday evening has a walking-street market.
items.tip: Walk Thalang Road and Soi Romanee, ideally on Sunday evening.
items.why: It shows the island's tin-mining and Chinese heritage, and has its best food.
flow: Start on Thalang Road.
Turn into Soi Romanee and on to Dibuk Road.

items.name: Big Buddha
items.summary: A 45-metre white marble Buddha on a hilltop, visible across the south of the island.
items.expect: Dress modestly; sarongs are lent at the entrance.
items.tip: Go early or late for cooler air.
items.why: It has sweeping views of Chalong Bay and the west coast.
flow: Drive or taxi up the hill.
Walk around the base terrace.

items.name: Promthep Cape
items.summary: The island's southern tip and its most popular sunset viewpoint.
items.expect: Crowds and tour buses at sunset.
items.tip: Walk down the path towards the tip to leave the crowd.
items.why: The classic place to watch the sun set into the Andaman Sea.
flow: Arrive 45 minutes before sunset.
Walk beyond the lighthouse.

items.name: Kata Noi Beach
items.summary: A small bay of fine sand and clear water at the quiet end of Kata.
items.expect: Limited parking and strong surf in monsoon months.
items.tip: Swim only between the flags; red flags mean stay out.
items.why: One of the island's prettiest swimming beaches in high season.
flow: Arrive in the morning for shade.
Swim, then go up to Karon Viewpoint.

items.name: Raya Restaurant
items.summary: A two-storey old mansion serving southern Thai and Phuket dishes.
items.expect: Simple service and busy evenings.
items.tip: Order the crab curry with rice vermicelli.
items.why: It is the classic place for Phuket home cooking.
flow: Reserve or come early.
Share crab curry, moo hong and stir-fried greens.
order: Crab meat curry with rice vermicelli

items.name: One Chun
items.summary: A retro café-restaurant for Phuket's Hokkien-influenced dishes at moderate prices.
items.expect: Queues at dinner.
items.tip: Go for lunch or put your name down early.
items.why: It is a reliable introduction to local Peranakan flavours.
flow: Take a queue number.
Order crab curry and stir-fried pork with shrimp paste.

items.name: Phuket Town Sunday Walking Street
items.summary: A Sunday evening street market of snacks, sweets and crafts under lit shophouses.
items.expect: Sunday only, about 4 pm to 10 pm; very busy.
items.tip: Graze: try o-aew shaved ice dessert and grilled skewers.
items.why: The best single evening for local snacks.
flow: Start at the Phuket Road end.
Snack your way along Thalang Road.

name: Hoi An
summary: A small riverside trading port, best seen on foot or by bicycle. Mornings in the old town, afternoons at the beach or in the rice fields, and evenings under the lanterns.
seasonNote: October and November bring heavy rain and frequent flooding in the old town.
arrival: Fly or take the train to Da Nang, then 45 minutes by taxi or shuttle.
gettingAround: The old town is closed to cars for much of the day; rent a bicycle for the beach and countryside.
cashTip: Carry dong for street food, markets and old town tickets; tailors and hotels take cards.
foodTip: Try cao lầu noodles, white rose dumplings, cơm gà chicken rice and a bánh mì.
buyTip: Tailored clothes (allow two fittings), silk lanterns and leather goods.
baseArea: Edge of the old town, or An Bang beach
via: Fly into Da Nang, then about 45 minutes by road

items.name: Hoi An Ancient Town
items.summary: A 15th to 19th-century trading port of ochre shophouses, assembly halls and lanterns.
items.expect: A ticket covers five heritage buildings; evenings are crowded.
items.tip: Walk it at 7 am before the groups arrive, then again after dark.
items.why: The whole town is a World Heritage site and unusually intact.
flow: Buy the old town ticket.
Visit Tan Ky house and the Fujian Assembly Hall.

items.name: Japanese Covered Bridge
items.summary: A small roofed bridge with a temple inside, built by Japanese merchants in the 1590s.
items.expect: Always busy for photos.
items.tip: See it lit at night from the riverside.
items.why: It is the symbol of Hoi An, shown on the 20,000 dong note.
flow: Cross with an old town ticket.
Step into the small temple on the north side.

items.name: My Son Sanctuary
items.summary: Brick temple towers of the Cham kingdom in a jungle valley, from the 4th to 13th centuries.
items.expect: Hot by mid-morning; many towers were damaged by bombing.
items.tip: Take a sunrise tour to arrive before the heat and buses.
items.why: It is the most important Cham site in Vietnam.
flow: Drive about an hour inland.
Walk the temple groups with a guide.

items.name: An Bang Beach
items.summary: A relaxed stretch of sand with loungers and seafood shacks, 5 km from town.
items.expect: Rough seas from October to February.
items.tip: Cycle there through the rice fields and buy lunch for a free lounger.
items.why: An easy beach break from the old town.
flow: Cycle out along Hai Ba Trung Street.
Take a lounger at a beach restaurant.

items.name: Tra Que Vegetable Village
items.summary: A farming village of herb gardens between town and beach, offering farming and cooking classes.
items.expect: Classes are touristy but hands-on.
items.tip: Cycle through for free, or book a half-day cooking class.
items.why: It grows the herbs that give Hoi An's dishes their flavour.
flow: Cycle the garden paths.
Join a farming and cooking session.

items.name: Lantern boat ride on the Thu Bon River
items.summary: A short evening ride in a small wooden boat hung with lanterns, releasing paper candles on the water.
items.expect: Dozens of boats at once; fixed prices are posted at the pier.
items.tip: Pay at the official ticket booth rather than bargaining with touts.
items.why: It is the classic Hoi An evening.
flow: Buy a ticket at the riverside booth.
Float past the lit old town for 20 minutes.

items.name: Bánh Mì Phượng
items.summary: The bánh mì shop made famous by Anthony Bourdain.
items.expect: A long queue at lunch and dinner.
items.tip: Go mid-morning and order the mixed special.
items.why: It is the best-known sandwich in Vietnam.
flow: Queue at the counter.
Order a number 9 mixed bánh mì.

items.name: Morning Glory
items.summary: A restaurant by local chef Trinh Diem Vy serving Hoi An street food classics.
items.expect: Popular with visitors; book for dinner.
items.tip: A good place to try cao lầu and white rose dumplings together.
items.why: It introduces the town's specialities in one comfortable sitting.
flow: Reserve for dinner.
Order cao lầu, white rose and bánh xèo.

items.name: Hoi An Central Market food hall
items.summary: A covered market with a food hall of small counters selling noodles and rice dishes.
items.expect: Vendors call you over; prices are posted.
items.tip: Have cao lầu or mì Quảng for breakfast.
items.why: The cheapest place to eat local dishes among locals.
flow: Pick a counter in the food hall.
Order a bowl of noodles.
